name: Design an Inventory Management System
intent: Track how many units of every product sit in every warehouse, promise them to shoppers without ever selling what does not exist, and keep websites, apps and stores in agreement while a flash sale hammers one product.
codeTitle: a stock ledger with expiring reservations and cycle counts
finalIntro: One checkout reserving stock, paying, and showing up in every channel, and a night-time count correcting a miss.
prompt: Design the inventory system for a retailer with 12 warehouses, a website, a mobile app, stores and marketplaces. It must know how many units of each product are available, hold stock for a shopper during checkout, never sell more than exists, handle a flash sale where tens of thousands of people want the same product, and stay correct when the shelves and the system disagree.
functional: Record every receipt, sale, return, transfer and correction of stock
Show how many units of a product are available, per warehouse and in total
Reserve units for a shopper during checkout, and give them back if the shopper does not pay in time
Choose which warehouse fulfils an order
Run cycle counts and fix the stock figures when the shelf and the system disagree
Tell every sales channel when availability changes
nonFunctional: Never sell a unit that does not exist, even when thousands of requests hit the same product at once
A reservation answers in under 100 ms, including during a flash sale
Availability shown on channels may lag by a few seconds, but a checkout is always checked against the real figure
Handle about 1,000 reservations per second overall, and tens of thousands per second for one hot product
Every change of stock can be explained: who, when, why
A warehouse or a channel being offline must not stop the others
Recover from a crash without losing or duplicating a movement

firstAttempt.text: One table with a row per product and warehouse holding a quantity. Checkout reads the quantity, and if it is enough, writes the quantity minus the order. Warehouses, the website and the stores all read and write that table directly.
limits: Two checkouts that read the same quantity at the same time both succeed, and the product is sold twice
Overwriting a number loses the history, so nobody can say why the figure is 14 and not 17
Nothing is held during checkout, so a shopper can be told the unit is gone after they have typed their card number
Everyone reads and writes the same rows, so a flash sale on one product locks out the others
When the shelf count differs from the number, there is no way to correct it except by overwriting, which hides what happened

steps.title: Record stock as a ledger of movements
steps.problem: A quantity that is overwritten forgets how it got there. When the figure is wrong nobody can tell whether a receipt was missed, a sale was counted twice or a unit was stolen.
steps.fix: Never edit the stock figure. Every change is an append-only movement: a receipt of +100 from a purchase order, a pick of -2 for an order, a return of +1, a transfer as a -5 in one warehouse and a +5 in another, a correction of -3 from a count. Each movement has a unique reference, so a retry of the same one is recognised and ignored. The balance for a product and warehouse is the sum of its movements, kept as a projection (a running total updated in the same transaction as the append) so that reading it is a single lookup.
steps.tradeoff: Every figure is explainable, the history can be replayed, and a bug in the projection is fixed by recomputing it. The ledger only grows, so old movements are summarised into periodic snapshots, and a read that must be exact needs the projection to be updated atomically with the append.

steps.title: Reserve units, and let reservations expire
steps.problem: Between 'add to basket' and 'payment confirmed' the shopper needs the unit to stay theirs, but a shopper who closes the tab must not hold it for ever.
steps.fix: A reservation is a hold of N units of a product in a warehouse, with an id, an owner and an expiry time such as ten minutes. Available stock is the balance minus the units held by active reservations. Paying turns the hold into a pick movement in the ledger. Letting it lapse, or cancelling, releases it. A timer service sweeps expired holds, and the expiry is also checked when someone tries to pay, so a hold that has just lapsed cannot be turned into a sale by a slow payment.
steps.tradeoff: Shoppers are not surprised at the last step, and abandoned baskets give their stock back automatically. A longer hold is kinder to shoppers and locks more stock, so the length is a business choice, and a payment that completes after expiry must be handled: try to hold again, and refund if the stock is gone.

steps.title: Make the check and the hold one atomic step
steps.problem: Two requests that read 'one left' at the same instant both decide to sell it. The check and the write must not be separable.
steps.fix: Do the check inside the write: 'hold 2 units if balance minus held is at least 2', as one conditional update on the counter row, which the database runs under a row lock or as a compare-and-set (write only if the version is unchanged) on a version. Exactly one of two competing requests wins and the other gets a clear 'not enough stock'. All stock counters for one product live on one shard (one slice of the database), chosen by a hash of the product id, so this atomic step never needs a distributed transaction.
steps.tradeoff: Overselling becomes impossible rather than unlikely, and the answer is immediate. Requests for the same product now queue on one row, which is fine at a few hundred per second and a problem at tens of thousands, so the hot product needs its own treatment.

steps.title: Publish changes as events to warehouses and channels
steps.problem: The website, the app, the stores and the marketplaces all need to know the figures, and each warehouse runs its own system. Making all of them read one database couples them to it, and asking them to update it in step is impossible when one is offline.
steps.fix: Writing a movement also writes an event to an outbox (a table of events saved with the change) in the same transaction, and a relay publishes it to an event bus, at least once and in order per product. Warehouses receive pick instructions from it, and report receipts and shipments back as movements. The channel sync builds each channel's view of availability from the events, with a safety buffer per channel (a marketplace sees 'available minus 5') and shows it a second or two late. The authority is still the reservation: a channel's number is only a hint, and the checkout is always checked against the real counter.
steps.tradeoff: Channels and warehouses are decoupled, and a slow one only falls behind. Displayed availability is briefly wrong, so a shopper may see 'in stock' and then be refused, which is acceptable if the refusal is polite and the sale is never wrong. Consumers see events more than once and must ignore repeats.

steps.title: Count the shelves and reconcile with the ledger
steps.problem: Shelves lose units to damage, theft and mistakes in picking. The system says 48, the shelf has 45, and the figure only gets worse until someone checks.
steps.fix: Cycle counting visits each product and location on a rotation, with fast sellers counted more often. A count is taken as of a ledger position, and the difference between the counted number and the balance at that position (plus the movements since) is written as a correction movement with a reason code and the counter's id, never as an overwrite. Variances above a threshold are flagged for a recount or a review. A nightly job also compares the projection with a replay of the ledger and the warehouse system's own figures, and reports every product where they disagree.
steps.tradeoff: Errors are found and fixed in a small area while they are small, and every correction is visible and attributable. Counting costs labour and sometimes pauses picking in an aisle, and a count taken while picks are in flight must be reconciled against the position it was taken at, or the adjustment will be wrong.

steps.title: Survive a flash sale on one product
steps.problem: When 20,000 requests per second target a single product, they all queue on one counter row. Most time out, and the stock may even be left unsold because shoppers gave up.
steps.fix: Three layers work together. A sale queue admits shoppers at the rate the stock can take, and gives the rest a place in line instead of an error. The hot product's stock is split into slices of a few hundred units, each in its own counter row, and a request picks a slice at random and tries one other on a miss, so many rows work in parallel. Once the total reaches zero a cached 'sold out' flag answers everything else at the edge without touching a counter.
steps.tradeoff: Throughput grows with the number of slices, shoppers see a line instead of errors, and the counters are never overloaded. A slice can run dry while others have stock, so a few shoppers may be told 'sold out' wrongly near the end unless the leftovers are rebalanced, and the sale queue adds a short wait.

failures.scenario: A shopper pays after the hold expired
failures.impact: The unit may already be reserved by someone else, so confirming the payment would oversell.
failures.answer: The payment step checks the hold's expiry and its state. If the hold lapsed, the service tries to take a new hold. If that works, the order goes ahead. If not, the payment is cancelled or refunded and the shopper is offered a similar item or a waiting list.

failures.scenario: A warehouse system goes offline for an hour
failures.impact: Receipts and shipments stop arriving, so the figures for that warehouse drift from the shelves.
failures.answer: Its events queue on the bus and are applied in order when it returns. Meanwhile the reservations service stops sourcing new orders from that warehouse if its feed is stale, falls back to others, and sets a bigger safety buffer for its stock on the channels. Reconciliation after recovery catches whatever slipped.

failures.scenario: The same stock event is delivered twice
failures.impact: A channel or a warehouse would count a receipt or a sale twice.
failures.answer: Each movement has a unique reference, and consumers record the references they have applied. Applying an event again is a no-op. Because the ledger itself rejects a duplicate reference, a producer that retries after a timeout cannot add a movement twice either.

failures.scenario: The reservation service crashes with thousands of holds open
failures.impact: If holds lived only in memory, they vanish, and the stock they covered could be sold again while the shoppers are still paying.
failures.answer: Holds are rows in the same store as the counters, written in the same transaction as the counter change, so they survive a restart. The expiry timers are rebuilt from the rows' expiry times when the service starts. A periodic check also compares the sum of active holds with the held figure on each counter and repairs any mismatch.

failures.scenario: A cycle count finds 40 units missing on a product with open orders
failures.impact: The balance drops below the units already held, so available stock goes negative and some paid orders cannot be fulfilled.
failures.answer: The correction is written as a movement like any other, so available goes negative and new reservations stop at once. Orders that cannot be fulfilled are re-sourced from other warehouses first, then the latest ones are backordered or cancelled with an apology. The variance is flagged for a review.

alternatives.title: How stock is stored

options.name: A mutable quantity per row
options.con: Forgets history, so errors cannot be explained or replayed

options.name: Ledger of movements with a projection
options.con: Two structures to keep consistent, and the ledger grows

options.name: Ledger only, summed on read
options.con: Too slow for a hot product without snapshots

alternatives.pick: Ledger of movements, plus a balance projection updated in the same transaction.

alternatives.title: How overselling is prevented

options.name: Pessimistic lock on the row
options.con: Callers queue, and a slow caller holds everyone up

options.name: Conditional update (compare and set)
options.pro: Short, no lock held across calls, clear failure

options.name: One in-memory owner per product
options.pro: Very fast, with no database contention
options.con: Needs a way to persist and fail over the owner

alternatives.pick: A conditional update on the database for most products, and slices or an owner for the hottest.

alternatives.title: When to reserve

options.name: On add to basket
options.con: Baskets abandoned by the thousand lock stock

options.name: At the start of checkout
options.pro: A short hold for shoppers who are serious
options.con: A shopper can still lose an item before checkout

options.name: At payment only
options.pro: Nothing is ever held for nothing
options.con: Shoppers learn about a stock-out after entering their card

alternatives.pick: Reserve at the start of checkout, for a few minutes.

alternatives.title: What to do when stock runs out

options.name: Never oversell
options.con: Some stock is held back, and sales are lost to caution

options.name: Allow a small oversell buffer
options.pro: Absorbs shrinkage and returns, so more is sold

options.name: Backorders
options.pro: Sales are kept, the shopper sees a date
options.con: Needs supplier lead times and clear messages

alternatives.pick: Never oversell on hot or limited products, and allow backorders where a resupply date is known.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The inventory API and the channel sync.

roles.label: Events and timers
roles.description: The event bus, expiry timers and the sale queue.

roles.label: State
roles.description: The ledger, the counters and the warehouse systems.

quiz.question: A product's stock table shows 14 units, but the shelf has 17. The table holds only a quantity that every sale and receipt overwrites. Nobody can tell whether a receipt was missed or a sale counted twice. Which redesign lets the team find the cause next time?
options: Add updated_at and updated_by columns to the row, so that the team can see who wrote the most recent value
Append each change as a movement with a unique reference, keep a running balance, and record fixes as movements
Copy the whole table into a snapshot every night, and compare the snapshots to find the day when the figure went wrong
Turn on the database statement log for the table and keep it for 30 days, so that the team can replay the writes
quiz.explanation: A ledger of movements explains every figure, can be replayed, and its unique references make retries safe. The last-writer columns show only the final change, nightly snapshots are too coarse to find one missed receipt, and a statement log is hard to read as business events and does not correct the count.

quiz.question: A flash sale offers 5,000 units of one product, and 20,000 requests per second arrive. All counters for the product are one row, which can take about 1,000 updates per second, so most requests time out. Which combination fixes this?
options: Raise the transaction isolation level of the counter update to serializable, so the database orders competing requests more safely
Move the database to a machine with more CPU and memory, so that it can update the single hot row faster than before
Split the stock into slices of a few hundred units, admit shoppers through a queue, and cache a sold-out flag
Retry each timed-out request up to five times with exponential backoff, so that every shopper eventually gets a turn
quiz.explanation: One row sets the limit, so the stock is sliced into rows that work in parallel and the queue sets the rate. Serializable isolation adds contention, a bigger machine barely speeds a single hot row, and retries multiply the load on the counter that is already the bottleneck.

quiz.question: A balance shows 100 units, with 70 held for open orders. A cycle count finds only 60 on the shelf. What should the system do with the 40 missing units?
options: Overwrite the balance with 60 and release 10 of the oldest holds, so that the available figure does not go below zero
Reject the count until the 70 held units have shipped, since a count taken during open orders cannot be trusted and the shelves are in flux
Write the correction only against the 30 unheld units, and keep the 70 held units untouched for the orders that are open
Write a -40 correction movement with a reason code, so available goes to -10 and new holds stop, then re-source 10 orders
quiz.explanation: The correction is a movement like any other: balance becomes 60, holds are 70, so available is -10 and new reservations stop at once. Orders short by 10 units are re-sourced, then backordered. Overwriting hides the cause and silently breaks promises, a count cannot wait since the shelves are the real stock, and limiting the fix to the 30 unheld units leaves the books 10 above the shelf.
